power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Trust in AI: A Decision-Theoretic framework for Human-AI Interactions in the Digital Society

text.text: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is crucial for ensuring productive human-AI interactions across domains ranging from medicine to finance.
As AI systems become central in the digital society, understanding how people decide when to rely on AI advice becomes increasingly important.
This paper proposes that a decision-theoretic perspective is needed to explain how well-calibrated trust in AI can be achieved.

We emphasize that an important component of trust in AI involves a decision to delegate control to an artificial agent, balancing potential rewards and risks of following AI advice versus relying on one's own judgment.

Framed this way, established decision-making theories such as Prospect Theory, Evidence Accumulation Models, and Reinforcement Learning offer valuable insights into the cognitive processes that underlie trust in AI.

These theories offer formal, computational models for explaining how individuals evaluate AI-generated advice, weigh risks and rewards, form biases, and update trust based on feedback, enabling precise hypotheses about when and why people accept or reject AI advice.

We offer several examples illustrating that grounding trust in cognitive theory provides a conceptual framework for empirical research that moves beyond surface-level behaviors and towards mechanistic understanding.

We conclude that a decision-theoretic approach can enhance psychological insight and guide the responsible design of AI systems within the digital society that are better aligned with human cognition.

The digital society we live in is infused with Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, which are capable of interacting with the environment and aim to simulate human intelligence (Glikson & Woolley, 2020).

text.text: Trust in AI is no less of an intricate concept as trust in general.

Initially, trust in AI was mainly considered in terms of technology acceptance. Davis (1989) assumes that the use of (new) technology is mainly determined by two variables: the perceived usefulness of technology and the perceived ease of use of technology.

text.text: Sustainable interactions with AI require that people balance their expectations, being neither too optimistic nor too skeptical but aligned with what an AI system can actually do.

This balance requires a certain degree of trust in the system, so to make optimal use of its potential, while also preventing over-trust that may lead to potentially devastating outcomes when errors are not detected in time.
Trust is appropriate when the user's trust formed by beliefs about the AI's trustworthiness is in line with the AI's actual trustworthiness.
To this end, trust needs to be calibrated or aligned to correct for over-and under-trust over the course of time and repeated interactions.
In line with technology acceptance, Mehrotra et al. (2024) map different trust constructs in terms of beliefs, intentions, and behavior, which results in a complex interplay of trust elements.

At the same time, users expect AI to uphold certain functionalities and trust is endorsed without any proof that AI system actually does what it is intended to do (i.e., contractual trust).
Of course, trust calibration will also depend on the perceived capability of AI.

Here, we propose that research on trust in AI and interventions aimed at optimizing trust in AI may benefit a lot by considering that trust in AI also involves a decision process.

Considering trust from a cognitive psychological perspective is not new (e.g., Chen et al., 2023; Delgado et al., 2023; McEvily, 2011) and its heuristic value in organizing the different trust constructs is acknowledged (PytlikZillig & Kimbrough, 2016).

text.text: However, at a deeper level of analysis the question remains what cognitive mechanisms support these processes?

Whereas research on Human-AI interaction often acknowledges that trust is mediated by human cognition, the exact cognitive mechanisms underlying acceptance behavior are often not specified and regarded as topics for more 'fundamental' cognitive neuroscientific research (e.g., Chang et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2023; Delgado et al., 2023).

text.text: Rather, our focus is on isolating one specific component of trust in AI: the decision process by which individuals choose whether, when, and to what extent to rely on AI systems.
We argue that this decision component is especially central in decision support systems, where trust is often expressed behaviorally through reliance or delegation.
In order to create a pathway for specifying and formalizing the cognitive processes underlying trust in AI, we propose to endorse a decision-theoretic perspective.

Such an approach relates, for instance, to earlier work on trust by McEvily (2011), who considered trust as form of social decision-making closely related to decision-making under risk that could either be analytical in nature or more automatic on the basis of heuristics formed by the trustor.

text.text: Here, we illustrate that a decision-making perspective enables us to relate trust in AI to three well-studied paradigms of decision making that can be formalized with computational models.
To this end, we focus on DSS.
The use of DSS is central in the domain of AI (see above) and is supported by a class of AI systems designed to provide predictive or prescriptive outputs in structured tasks (Wang et al., 2019).

text.text: In DSS -contrary to more exploratory or co-creative human-AI interactions -the outcomes of a decision can be readily evaluated, and the stakes are well-defined.
In particular, DSS allow individual to either accept the advice that is provided by the DSS, or reject it.
Although this offers a well-delineated framework for the present purposes, we acknowledge that trust in AI takes different forms and goes beyond such interactions.
We consider the benefit of our approach for broader types of Human-AI interactions and trust research in general later on.

In order to build a strong decision-theoretic framework on trust in AI, we focus on a specific aspect of trust that is especially relevant in human-AI interaction: the decision to accept or reject AI advice.
Rather than redefining trust itself, we isolate the decision component of trust that governs reliance behavior in situations involving AI-supported decision making.
To this end, we define the acceptance or rejection of AI advice as a decision-making process.

More specifically, we conceptualize this reliance decision as the decision to outsource some degree of control in a particular situation to AI in order to achieve a particular outcome that has more value than when no control is outsourced, but with the risk of getting a higher penalty than when control is not outsourced (cf. PytlikZillig & Kimbrough, 2016).

text.text: That is, someone may choose to trust AI and for example accept decision support.
They do so expecting a better outcome than when making a decision alone.
At the same time, they release control over the action that will be decided upon.
The critical reader may argue that our definition of trust is not entirely new and contains elements that were iterated before.
The brief overview provided in the previous section also indicates that our definition misses elements.
Instead, we aim to isolate the component of trust that manifests in observable reliance decisions and that can be modeled using decision-theoretic tools.

text.text: In each case, users choose to either delegate control to AI or ignore its recommendation and make their own judgment.
By outsourcing, we can save time (e.g., avoiding the need to search for series or holiday destinations ourselves) or gain certainty (e.g., receiving a 'second opinion' in medical diagnoses).
However, there is also the risk that the AI's advice may not meet our expectations (e.g., suggesting unwatchable series, bad hotels, or an incorrect diagnosis).
Similarly, for more socially-geared interactions with AI, sharing personal information with a mental-health bot involves outsourcing control of this information to AI in order to achieve help.
However, a potential risk is that this personal information could be misused.

text.text: Here, we illustrate how Prospect Theory, Evidence Accumulation Models (EAMs), and Reinforcement Learning (RL) -offer hypotheses and concrete predictions about trust in AI by making specific assumptions about the cognitive mechanisms underlying trust in AI and trust in general.
We briefly introduce each framework and consider it in view of DSS.
Next, we formulate some predictions -some of which are already tested.
However, we emphasize that we do not provide an exhaustive list of predictions.
Other hypotheses could be entertained based on different literature, yielding different predictions.
This follows from an important distinction between hypotheses and theoretical frameworks.
The framework enables formulation of the specific hypothesis, but there may be others as well.

In the context of cognitive models, this distinction is well-known (Cooper, 2007): A framework allows for the coherent study of certain fields (in this case, decision-making, including decisions about following AI advice) and it allows for the derivation of explicit hypotheses that can be subsequently tested.

text.text: Rejection of specific hypotheses should not lead to the dismissal of the complete framework however, but only to the dismissal of the specific hypothesis.
The decision to accept AI advice can be viewed as a choice between risky prospects.
The most well-known paradigm in which risky decision making has been studied is Prospect Theory (Fox & Poldrack, 2009; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Tversky & Kahneman, 1992).

text.text: Prospect Theory postulates that decisions are based on the perceived utility of each option, weighted by their perceived probabilities.
This can result in individuals choosing a less desirable but more likely option over a more desirable, less likely option, avoiding the risk of ending up empty handed.
In addition, Prospect Theory assumes that individuals differ in how they value certain alternatives, and that individuals have no ideal insight into probabilities.
These assumptions help to explain why people often deviate from a normatively optimal choice.

In particular, people tend to be risk-seeking in the loss domain -that is, when there is a chance of a negative outcome -and risk-averse in the gain domain, when there is a chance of a positive outcome (Fox & Poldrack, 2009; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Ruggeri et al., 2020).

text.text: Prospect Theory and the impact of risk and loss aversion in advice acceptance in DSS are starting to gain attraction and offer a promising pathway for obtaining new insights on trust in AI.

For example, following Prospect Theory, users may be more likely to reject AI advice in gain-framed contexts due to risk aversion, but may accept AI advice more readily when outcomes are framed as losses.
This hypothesis is based on similar observations in non-AI contexts, where participants have to make judgments framed as gains or losses respectively (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Ruggeri et al., 2020).

Other studies observed that algorithms are relied upon more when decisions lead to gain, but not when the outcome is a loss (Toma et al., 2020) or did not obtain any evidence that outcome framing influences the acceptance of algorithmic advice (Liefooghe et al., 2026).

text.text: Moreover, Dietvorst and Bharti (2020) consider outcome probability and risk taking in the context of algorithm aversion by proposing that the sensitivity to a DSS error decreases when these errors are more frequent.
This entails that DSS are evaluated on the basis of the perceived likelihood of producing a near-perfect outcome rather than on the DSS's average level of performance.

They found that for uncertain decision domains human support is preferred over algorithms, because the higher variability associated with human performance is perceived as offering a greater opportunity of achieving a near-perfect outcome by chance.
The corresponding disadvantage of being more likely to be very inaccurate, receives less weight, in line with the asymmetric weighting of gains and losses that is predicted by Prospect Theory.
In contrast, algorithms are perceived as being more consistent and less variable, which makes it unlikely that a near-perfect outcome can be obtained by chance.
However, these differences in expectations toward human and algorithmic forecasters were found to be mitigated when the uncertainty of the decision domain increases.
Under such conditions the outcome uncertainty becomes so high that the effect of forecast variability is negligible and preferences for human and algorithmic forecasters become similar.

Whereas initial evidence supports this account (Dietvorst & Bharti, 2020), additional research indicates that when an outcome is very unlikely algorithms are even preferred over human support (Liefooghe et al., 2026).

text.text: Taken together, viewing advice taking from AI through the lens of Prospect Theory suggests that trust in AI is fundamentally shaped by how decision makers perceive and evaluate risk and uncertainty rather than by objective system performance alone.

Whether AI advice is accepted depends not only on expected accuracy, but also on how potential gains and losses are framed, how uncertain outcomes are perceived, and how people weigh the risks of relying on AI versus relying on their own judgment.

Consequently, trust in AI can be viewed as a context-dependent decision process in which subjective evaluations of risk, uncertainty, and outcome framing jointly determine whether control is delegated to an AI system.
Furthermore, Prospect Theory generates new hypotheses regarding trust in AI.
For instance, the subjective value of accepting advice (one's own, another human expert, or an AI system) may vary, influencing the acceptance rate of AI advice (Tversky & Kahneman, 1992).

A second important paradigm when considering trust in AI as a decision-making process is the Evidence Accumulation Model (EAM).
The dynamics of decision-making processes have been extensively investigated using these models (Mulder et al., 2014; Ratcliff et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The dynamics of decision-making processes have been extensively investigated using these models <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Mulder et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Ratcliff et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: EAMs assume that, in order to select a choice alternative, individuals accumulate evidence over time for the choice alternatives, reaching a threshold that supports one alternative over the other.
The alternative that first reaches this threshold is selected.
The speed of evidence accumulation is determined by the difficulty of the decision (e.g., Heekeren et al., 2004; Mulder et al., 2013; Van Maanen et al., 2016).

text.text: When evidence takes the form of the difference in expected utilities between two options, a choice becomes more difficult when the expected utilities are more comparable (Summerfield & Tsetsos, 2012).

text.text: In contrast, when the expected utilities of the alternatives are clearly dissimilar, decision makers are quick to select the most desirable choice alternative.
The effectiveness and relevance of EAMs in investigating trust in AI lie in their ability to identify and quantify the cognitive mechanisms that control the speed and accuracy of decisions.
Two main processes drive these dynamics.
First, decision makers are believed to have control over the decision threshold, when they feel this is appropriate in a given situation (Bogacz et al., 2010; Van Maanen et al., 2011).

text.text: The consequence of a higher threshold is that the likelihood of selecting the best option increases, but decisions take longer (Boehm et al., 2020; Bogacz et al., 2006).

text.text: Inversely, a lower threshold allows for faster decisions, but results in more variable -and possibly incorrect -choices.

This mechanism provides a natural explanation of the often observed speed-accuracy trade-off in decision making (Heitz, 2014), in which individuals in daily life or professional environments such as medical diagnoses or financial trading, must balance the need for quick decisions with the importance of a correct choice.

text.text: A second process involves decision makers having a prior preference for one choice alternative over the others, which according to the EAM paradigm yields asymmetric decision behavior.

A prior preference means that less additional evidence is required to reach the decision threshold for the favored alternative, accelerating the decision-making process for that option while delaying decisions for the other options (Cerracchio et al., 2023; Leite & Ratcliff, 2011; Mulder et al., 2012; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; White & Poldrack, 2014).

text.text: These mechanisms potentially explain the decision to trust AI across different contexts, where factors influence the need for speed or accuracy, or when initial preferences for a certain outcome affect the decision-making process.
With respect to algorithm aversion, a hypothesis could be that shifted starting points may reflect a discrepancy in trust, where individuals have a bias to disagree with AI.
Such a mechanism would result in rapid, habitual rejections of AI advice even when evidence supports accepting it.
Such a mechanisms would be in line with findings that show that expectations of differential reward lead to choice biases (Bogacz et al., 2006; Mulder et al., 2012).

text.text: However, an alternative EAM explanation of algorithm aversion could be that the choice to agree with AI simply requires more evidence, for example because individuals find it less trustworthy.
In a medical decision-making experiment, we indeed found evidence for this second hypothesis (Van Maanen et al., 2025).

text.text: In two experiments, we asked participants to indicate whether they agreed or disagreed with the assessment of x-ray images by a medical advisor.
In one experimental condition, the advisor was framed as a human, whereas in the other condition, the advisor was framed as an algorithm.
We found that in the algorithmic-advice condition, participants indeed had a higher threshold, resulting in slower choices, and fewer incorrect choices.
This pattern was independent of whether the human advisor was framed as an expert radiologist or a naïve fellow participant.

This study this shows that measuring decision times alongside choices can help disentangle accumulation rates from starting point bias, shedding light on the decision mechanisms related to algorithm aversion.
A novel prediction that immediately follows from the EAM paradigm is that the difference between human and AI advice is mediated by time pressure.
That is, time pressure is believed to affect the decision threshold (Bogacz et al., 2010; Heitz, 2014; Van Maanen et al., 2011).

text.text: In this paradigm, after each decision, the value of an action or choice is updated, based on the mismatch between the expected and actual outcome.

A large mismatch between the expected and observed outcomes indicates that the value of an action has not yet been fully learned, resulting in an update of the expected outcome in the direction of the observed outcome.

Indeed, evidence from trust research suggests that trust develops through iterative feedback-based learning. Chang et al. (2010) demonstrated that trustworthiness judgments in repeated social interactions can be captured using computational learning models, showing that trust is updated dynamically as a function of prediction errors.

text.text: Applied to human-AI interaction, this finding suggests that trust in AI may be similarly shaped by repeated experiences with algorithmic performance, where prediction errors drive adjustments in beliefs about AI competence and reliability.
The RL paradigm thus provides an important perspective on trust in AI as it helps to explain how individuals learn to trust AI over time.
That is, it explains the underlying processes that results in a learned preference for one option over another, based on the outcomes of previous decisions.
As such, in the context of trust in AI, Reinforcement Learning helps us understand how individuals adjust their expectations about the reliability of algorithmic advice over time.

This is achieved by updating their trust as they observe whether the algorithm's recommendations lead to (un)expected or (un)preferred outcomes, which in turn can result in algorithm appreciation or aversion.

The speed at which new information is integrated into the existing value representation, called the learning rate, determines how quickly individuals adjust their beliefs in response to new information.
As such, this learning rate reflects how certain factors can affect the speed with which users adapt their trust, based on the performance of a DDS.

In addition to the learning rate, RL models include mechanisms that manage the trade-off between exploring new options and exploiting known ones (R. S. Sutton & Barto, 2018; van Maanen & Miletić, 2021).

The present discussion paper examines trust in AI through the lens of decision-making.
Specifically, we focused on the decision component of trust: the cognitive process through which individuals decide whether and to what extent to rely on AI advice.
This perspective is parsimonious and offers a common working ground for the multi-disciplinary field of AI.
More importantly, it offers the opportunity to further integrate psychological theory in the optimization of Human-AI interaction (see also Brysbaert, in press for the importance of doing so).

text.text: Specifically, a decision-theoretic approach can be developed to investigate and calibrate trust in AI, using three established paradigms: Prospect Theory, Evidence Accumulation Models and Reinforcement Learning.

These paradigms go beyond more general conceptualizations of human cognition that are often considered and offer formal, computational models that capture cognitive processes in a straightforward way that underly the decision to accept or reject AI advice.
As such, they can provide precise insights into how users evaluate and adjust their appreciation or aversion against AI systems in general, and DSS in particular.

After understanding these processes, a next step is to understand which moderating factors affect these processes (Proctor & Vu, 2010), and thereby mitigate the adverse effects of algorithm aversion or over-appreciation.

text.text: One approach to achieve this may be to study how the cognitive processes involved in trust in AI relate to the dispositional, situational, and learned aspects of trust (Hoff & Bashir, 2015).

text.text: Individual differences and personality traits can be considered with respect to the value assigned to a particular outcome and the perceived risk when outsourcing control to AI.
As such, AI may be appraised differently across individuals.
In addition, situational aspects can influence the decision to outsource control as well.
For instance, tasks and situations may vary in difficulty or urgency, which may influence the trustor's inclination to outsource.

Finally, the decision to outsource control evolves over repeated interactions with the AI system, which may facilitate learning that AI advice leads to a better outcome, resulting in an increased reliance on its advice.
Presumably, most cognitive mediators reflect all three elements.

For example, while it seems straightforward to assume that the learning rate of RL models is associated with learned aspects of trusts, individual differences in learning rate may reflect dispositional aspects, and different learning rates between different instances of a decision support system may reflect situational aspects.
The current paper focuses on trust in AI in the context of DSS.
These systems are characterized by structured tasks, evaluable outcomes, and well-defined stakes, which makes the application of decision theories and models relatively straightforward.
Unlike exploratory or co-creative human-AI interactions, DSS contexts more readily allow researchers to isolate decision variables, compute expected utilities, and apply normative benchmarks.

Moreover, the consequences of mis-calibrated trust such as over-reliance on faulty diagnostic tools or unwarranted rejection of accurate recommendations are particularly consequential in these domains.
As such, DSS provide both theoretical tractability and practical relevance for modeling accepting AI advice from a decision-theoretic perspective.
However, more complex interactions can also be considered, such as, in a joint-decision making setting.

Understanding these kinds of human-AI interactions may benefit from theories rooted in social psychology or sociology that address how individuals behave in the presence of others (e.g., with respect to the feeling of autonomy, Sankaran et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023).

text.text: Although the present paper focuses on developing a conceptual framework rather than prescribing specific experimental paradigms, the proposed models naturally lend themselves to empirical testing.
Prospect Theory predictions can be evaluated through manipulations of gain/loss framing and perceived AI reliability.
EAMs require joint analysis of choices and response times to distinguish bias from caution.
Reinforcement Learning models are particularly suited to repeated interaction paradigms in which trust evolves as a function of feedback.
Together, these approaches provide multiple avenues for empirically testing the cognitive mechanisms underlying trust in AI.
Nevertheless, the current work is not to argue in favor of Prospect Theory, the EAM paradigm, or RL modeling.
Rather, we advocate to consider the strong theoretical basis in the field of decision-making -including computational modeling -when considering trust decisions in the context of AI.

That is, one could also aim to study trust decisions using the heuristics and biases framework (Gigerenzer & Todd, 1999), or from the perspective of bounded rationality (Simon, 1997), and make use of the theoretical insights that are established with those frameworks.

text.text: Of course, our decision-theoretic approach of trust in AI only constitutes a very small piece in a far more complex puzzle.
This is because trust in AI unfolds within sociotechnical environments that also define what counts as trustworthy.
Trust in AI is thus not only a psychological construct as we treat it here, but also a social construct that allows individuals to act under uncertainty and complexity (Luhmann, 1979).

text.text: At the core of this process, we propose a decision-making mechanism that can possibly be moderated by the different constructs associated with trust.
Here, we considered the case of trust in AI, but future work may also try to apply our decision-theoretic approach to trust research more generally.

Our framework should therefore be understood as addressing one analytically tractable layer of trust-namely, reliance decisions under uncertainty-rather than the full phenomenon of trust in a digital society.

This five-stage framework maps naturally onto trust decisions involving AI systems.
Representation corresponds to identifying the task context, available control options, AI capabilities, and relevant uncertainties.
Valuation involves estimating the expected benefits and risks of delegating control to the AI relative to retaining human control.
Action selection is the trust decision itself-whether and to what extent control is outsourced.
Outcome evaluation assesses whether the AI's performance produced the expected outcome and whether trust was justified.
Learning updates beliefs about AI competence, reliability, and risk, shaping future trust decisions.
Thus, trust can be understood as a recurring value-based delegation process under uncertainty.
